## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Boles (2026) is now the best available national, school-level, course-by-course map of where AP STEM coursework was authorized in U.S. public high schools in 2015–2019, and the field should read it as exactly that: a verified descriptive landscape, not an adjusted-effect study. Its descriptive spine is unusually trustworthy. The College Board audit file covers the full population of 21,139 public high schools with non-offering schools added back, and every figure the sub-reviews recomputed from Tables 1 and 3 — roughly forty numbers across national rates, locale shares, and disproportionality gaps — reproduces to the decimal. The core facts need no modeling and can be cited with confidence: 48.0% of rural high schools obtained no AP STEM authorization in any of four years versus 20.9% of suburban schools; rural schools are 37.7% of high schools but 20.7% of those offering four or more courses; the deficit widens monotonically with the course-count threshold; and, unadjusted, rural and town schools trail on every one of the twelve courses, least in AP Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry. The caveats attach precisely to the paper's most quotable material. The headline that suburban schools offer 'nearly three times as many' AP STEM courses as rural schools (5.35 vs. 1.81) sits inside the adjusted-analysis section and is labeled as controlled, but three sub-reviews independently showed it cannot be a covariate-adjusted contrast — the implied structural-zero probabilities contradict the Model B coefficients it is attributed to, and it is in substance the raw locale gap. The size-adjusted count gap is about 14%, or roughly 0.8 courses. The school-size result — adding enrollment flips the sign of every locale coefficient in the zero-inflation model — is real and the paper's strongest analytic finding, but enrollment is partly constitutive of rurality rather than a confounder of it, so Model B decomposes the gap rather than dissolving it, and the widely quotable 'rural schools are 28.8% more likely to offer AP Calculus AB' is a product of that conditioning in a region of the covariate space where rural and suburban schools barely overlap. The abstract overstates the per-course result (Calculus AB reverses under controls and four courses show negligible adjusted gaps; the honest count is about eight of twelve, not eleven) and omits the size finding entirely; the by-course severity ranking holds on the odds scale but roughly reverses on the percentage-point scale; the AP Physics C: E&M column that carries the largest headline gap shows signs of quasi-separation; and the GWLR maps behind the fifth headline finding rest on estimates the paper deliberately withholds. Full reproduction is not possible from the published record — no code, no covariate descriptives, no audit-to-NCES crosswalk, no definition of the school universe (which appears to differ from prior national estimates: 66.7% of city schools offering an AP STEM course here versus the 88% the paper itself quotes from Mann et al.) — though the printed tables leave the descriptive claims fully auditable. Bottom line for the field: cite the tables, not the abstract; quote the unadjusted gaps as the policy-relevant facts and the adjusted ones as mechanism evidence about scale; treat the numbers as a pre-pandemic, pre-AP-Precalculus baseline; and watch for the audit-to-enrollment validation and finer rurality measures the paper plainly sets up.

#### Key Strengths

- Population coverage with a verifiable descriptive core: all 21,139 U.S. public high schools, the full College Board audit file for 2015–2019, non-offering schools added back so the denominator is the whole population — and every descriptive number in the prose reproduces exactly from Tables 1 and 3, which is rare enough to materially raise trust in the tables.
- The course-by-course disaggregation (Table 3 unadjusted, Table 4 with state fixed effects and school controls) is, as far as any sub-reviewer could determine, the first national school-level estimate for all twelve AP STEM subjects, and it yields the paper's most useful novel finding: locale gaps are subject-specific — smallest in core-adjacent courses, largest in calculus-based physics, Calculus BC, and Computer Science A — with city schools leading on CS Principles and Environmental Science.
- The Model A / Model B contrast in Table 2 confronts the school-size-versus-rurality confound head-on rather than assuming it away, and the sign flip on all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflation component is a clean, informative decomposition of where the extensive-margin locale gap comes from.
- The spatial layer does real work: rural schools in CT, DE, MD, MA, and NJ show a county median of four or more AP STEM courses while rural schools in 23 states have a median of zero, which establishes that 'rural' is not one condition and earns the paper's well-argued critique of NCES locale codes in the limitations section.
- Reporting transparency is above field norms in several respects — software down to package versions, full coefficient tables with standard errors, AIC/BIC and Brier scores, an explicit statement that inference is not the point with population data, a candid audit-versus-enrollment limitation, and a deposited openICPSR data-access guide for the restricted College Board file.

#### Key Concerns

- The paper's most quotable number is not the estimand it is labeled as. The combined ZIP predictions (suburb 5.35, city 3.64, town 2.41, rural 1.81) imply structural-zero probabilities of roughly .09/.36/.51/.64 that flatly contradict Model B's zero-inflation coefficients, under which rural schools of a given size have lower odds of a structural zero than suburban schools. These are locale-specific marginal predictions that track the raw Table 1 gap; the genuinely adjusted count gap is about 14% (0.8 courses). Expect 'nearly three times as many, controlling for school characteristics' to be cited, and do not repeat it.
- School size is treated as a confounder but is closer to a mediator of rurality. Model B answers 'do rural schools trail suburban schools of the same enrollment?' (no — on the extensive margin they do slightly better), which is a mechanism finding, not the policy-relevant contrast, and 'school size accounts for much of the relationship' is not licensed by comparing raw coefficients across two logit-link models (noncollapsibility, no decomposition, no locale × size interaction, no common-support diagnostic). The rural AP Calculus AB 'advantage' (+28.8% odds against an unadjusted 37.9% vs. 72.8%) is an extrapolation produced entirely by this conditioning.
- The abstract and the prose outrun the tables in specific, quotable places: the abstract's 'likelihood of offering each course' is contradicted by Calculus AB; '11 of the 12 courses' is really about eight, since Biology, Chemistry (rural), and CS Principles show negligible adjusted gaps and town Calculus AB and city CS Principles are within two standard errors of zero; the 'high-math-demand' category is never enumerated and footnote 10's definition sweeps in Calculus AB and Statistics while excluding CS A; the severity ranking is an odds-scale artifact that reverses on the percentage-point scale (Statistics, Chemistry, and Biology have the largest rural–suburban point gaps; the physics C courses the smallest); and Figures 2 and 8 carry x-axis labels describing a quantity they do not plot.
- Two parts of the modeling should be quoted only directionally. The AP Physics C: E&M logit — the column carrying the paper's largest headline gap — has an intercept of −25.9 and a log(proportion Asian) standard error ten times its neighbors, the signature of quasi-separation on the state fixed effects. The GWLR analysis behind the fifth headline finding reports no coefficients, bandwidth, kernel, or uncertainty (footnote 4), drops the state fixed effects used everywhere else (footnote 12), and yet supports state-specific claims about Iowa, South Carolina, New York, Vermont, and Maine that no reader can check. The 'structural zero' / 'no capacity' language throughout reifies a latent mixture class as a measured school attribute.
- The analysis cannot be rebuilt from the published record even with data access: no code in any form; no descriptive statistics for any covariate (so none of the predicted counts can be regenerated); an undocumented audit-to-NCES crosswalk whose unmatched records would land in the zero category that anchors the size finding; an undefined school universe (the 66.7% city rate in Table 1 versus the 88% the paper quotes from Mann et al. 2017 signals a materially different denominator); unreported constants inside the log transformations; an unexplained identical N across fourteen models; and no robustness checks — not even the twelve-category locale codes the paper holds and argues should matter.

#### What to Rely On

- The unadjusted locale gaps in AP STEM availability, 2015–2019 (Table 1): 79.1% of suburban, 66.7% of city, 63.3% of town, and 48.0% of rural public high schools obtained at least one AP STEM authorization; 7,982 schools (37.8%), 4,141 of them rural, obtained none in any of four years. These are population counts, verified to reproduce, and require no modeling.
- Rural underrepresentation widens with breadth: rural schools are 37.7% of high schools but 20.7% of those offering four or more AP STEM courses and 15.5% of rural schools reach five or more versus 58.8% of suburban schools (Table 1, Figure 2).
- Every AP STEM course is offered by a smaller share of rural and town schools than suburban schools unadjusted (Table 3), with the smallest relative rural deficits in Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry and the largest suburban overrepresentation in Physics C: E&M (+29.4 points of composition share), Physics C: Mechanics (+26.6), Physics 2 (+24.7), CS A (+23.7), and Calculus BC (+22.4) (Figure 8) — cite these as composition-share disproportionalities, not as gaps in offering rates.
- Locale gaps are subject-specific rather than uniform, and the ordering on the adjusted odds scale (Table 4, Figure 9) is genuinely largest for Physics C: E&M, Calculus BC, Physics 2, Physics C: Mechanics, and CS A and smallest for Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry — provided the claim is stated on the odds scale and the E&M magnitudes are treated as approximate.
- School enrollment is the dominant school-level correlate of whether a school holds any AP STEM authorization, and adding it reverses the sign of all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflation model (Table 2, Model A → B: city .375 → −.038, rural .341 → −.363, town .019 → −.192) — cite this as a decomposition showing the extensive-margin locale gap operates through scale, not as evidence that the gap disappears.
- Conditional on having a program, rural and town schools offer about 14–16% fewer AP STEM courses than suburban schools with the same enrollment and sociodemographics, and city schools about 3% fewer (Table 2, Model B count component) — the paper's genuinely adjusted intensive-margin gap, roughly 0.8 of a course.
- Rurality has heterogeneous curricular implications by region: rural schools in CT, DE, MD, MA, and NJ have a county median of four or more AP STEM courses while rural schools in 23 states (three Southern, eight Midwestern, twelve Western) have a median of zero (Figure 4). This is a county-level descriptive, not a GWLR result, and supports the paper's argument that NCES locale codes obscure rural heterogeneity.
- The paper's arithmetic. Every percent change quoted from Tables 2 and 4 (45.5/40.6/1.9; 3.41/14.14/15.90; 28.8/17.8/14.0/21.1), every national offering rate, and every disproportionality figure recomputes correctly; the one slip is a label ('AP Physics C: Magnetism' for Mechanics, p. 13). Numbers pulled from this paper's tables can be trusted.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'Suburban schools offer more than twice as many AP STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools' (p. 12) as an adjusted finding — the combined predictions are inconsistent with the Model B coefficients as a common-covariate contrast and are effectively the raw gap; cite Table 1 for the descriptive gap and the ~14% count-model contrast for the adjusted one.
- 'Rural schools have 28.8% higher odds of offering AP Calculus AB than suburban schools' — true only after conditioning on enrollment in a region with little rural–suburban overlap; unadjusted, 37.9% of rural versus 72.8% of suburban schools offer it. The defensible claim is that Calculus AB is the course where the rural deficit is proportionally smallest.
- 'Gaps are largest for high-math-demand courses' (abstract) — the category is never enumerated, footnote 10's definition includes Calculus AB (the reversed exception) and Statistics (mid-pack) while excluding CS A (in the largest-gap list), and the ranking holds only on the odds scale; on the percentage-point scale the largest rural–suburban deficits are Statistics (40.8 pp), Chemistry (37.6), and Biology (36.9), and the physics C courses are the smallest (13.4 and 20.9).
- 'Rural and town schools are still less likely to offer each AP STEM course, with the exception of AP Calculus AB' / '11 of the 12 courses' — Biology (rural −.024, town −.049), Chemistry (rural −.123), and CS Principles (rural −.134, town −.250) are indistinguishable from zero in Table 4, and the cited town Calculus AB (+17.8%) and city CS Principles (+14.0%) 'exceptions' are unstarred; read Figure 9's confidence intervals alongside every per-course sentence on pp. 14–15.
- 'School size accounts for much of the relationship between locale and structural support' — a raw coefficient comparison across two logit-link models with no decomposition; the 'odds ratio nearly halves' framing describes a sign reversal (OR 1.41 → 0.70), and Model B's rural coefficient means rural schools of a given size are less likely to be structural zeros, a sentence the paper never writes.
- Any magnitude from the AP Physics C: E&M column of Table 4 (rural −.562, town −.905) — the −25.9 intercept and the tenfold-inflated Asian-proportion standard error indicate quasi-separation; the direction is plausible, the precision is not.
- The state-specific GWLR claims (Iowa, South Carolina, New York, Vermont, Maine; pp. 15, 18) and Figures 10–11 generally — no estimates, bandwidth, or uncertainty are reported and state fixed effects are dropped; read as hypothesis-generating cartography.
- 'No structural support,' 'no capacity for AP STEM courses,' and 'schools with capacity' — labels for a latent ZIP mixture class identified by functional form alone; nothing in the data measures capacity, IB/DE reliance, or AP-program absence, and the audit file could have validated this (non-STEM AP audits with zero STEM audits) but was not used to.
- This paper's percentages placed next to other national AP-availability figures (Mann et al. 2017, Malkus 2016, NCES 2009) — the 21,139-school universe is never defined and appears to include alternative, virtual, and special-purpose schools that other estimates exclude (66.7% of city schools with an AP STEM course here versus the 88% quoted from Mann et al. on p. 5, in a measure that should be more generous, not less).
- Figures 2 and 8 — both x-axes say 'Percent of U.S. Public High Schools' but plot each locale's share of the course-offering subset; within-locale offering rates are in Tables 1 and 3, not in these figures. Figures 6 and 7 do not share a value domain despite the text saying the gradient is identical.
- The predicted course counts (5.869; 5.35/3.64/2.41/1.81) and anything downstream of them (Figures 6–7 choropleths) — no covariate means or fixed-effect convention are reported, so they are unverifiable and it is unstated whether the maps show count-only or combined predictions.
- Current-day relevance, especially for computer science — AP CS Principles launched in 2016–17, so its rural deficit partly measures rollout; AP Precalculus, state CS mandates, and post-2020 virtual AP delivery all postdate the window. Treat this as a 2015–2019 baseline.
- The discussion's dismissal of online delivery (p. 19) — sourced to COVID emergency-remote-instruction studies rather than to designed online AP programs (Hart et al. 2023 and Mader et al. 2025, which the paper cites only as future work), and in tension with footnote 2's implication that externally delivered AP is credited to whichever school completes the audit.
- The outcome itself — 'authorized to use the AP label in any of four years' is neither point-in-time availability nor a course actually taught nor enrollment; the paper says so, and a four-year zero is strong evidence of unavailability, but positive counts overstate what any student experienced in any year.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

Boles provides useful national evidence that rural and town public high schools have less extensive authorized AP STEM curricula than suburban schools, with important differences across subjects (p. 7, Table 1; p. 14, Table 3). The measured outcome is authorization at any point during the pooled historical study period, not annual course delivery or students' realized access (p. 5, Measures; p. 20, Limitations). The most valuable extension of the existing literature is school-level, subject-specific detail: adjusted rural and town shortfalls remain pronounced in advanced physics and Calculus BC, while Calculus AB reverses direction and Biology contrasts are small and uncertain (p. 16, Table 4). My overall judgment is useful with caveats: cite the descriptive patterns and carefully qualified subject-specific associations, but do not rely on the paper to establish causal mechanisms, observed institutional capacity, or effective remedies. Unexplained standardization of overall predicted course counts, weakly documented local spatial estimates, and prose that sometimes obscures adjusted exceptions limit stronger conclusions. These concerns narrow the contribution without overturning its national descriptive findings.

#### Key Strengths

- Broad national coverage includes schools without AP authorizations, and the descriptive tables report locale denominators alongside course counts and percentages, making the central comparisons directly auditable (p. 5, Data and Sample; p. 7, Table 1; p. 14, Table 3).
- Subject-specific models add substantive detail to the aggregate disparity: the relationship between locale and authorization differs between Calculus AB, Biology, Calculus BC, and advanced physics (p. 16, Table 4). My judgment is that this differentiation is the paper's strongest contribution.
- State fixed effects and school demographic adjustments contextualize the national comparisons; presenting course-count models with and without enrollment makes sensitivity to school size visible (p. 10, Table 2; p. 16, Table 4).
- The interdisciplinary framing distinguishes availability from accessibility and participation, recognizes prior geographic-disparity research, and acknowledges alternative advanced-course pathways and the limitations of authorization data (pp. 2–5, 20). This supports reading the paper as a useful extension of existing evidence.
- The paper specifies its national model structure and software and documents a data-use restriction with a linked access guide (pp. 6–7, 21). These are meaningful transparency provisions, although they do not establish exact reproducibility.

#### Key Concerns

- Measurement limits the central claim: pooled authorization can include intermittent or unrealized offerings, and school-weighted comparisons do not measure the share of students able to enroll. Other advanced-course pathways and outcomes are outside the analysis (p. 5, Measures; p. 20, Limitations).
- The reported overall predicted course-count gap lacks a defined standardization procedure. The text first says 'Holding socio-demographic variables at suburban means' and then says that combining model components makes 'the gulf in average AP STEM course count further widens' (p. 12, narrative predictions based on Table 2, p. 10). The reported suburban and rural predictions, 5.35 and 1.81, cannot be common-covariate comparisons under the printed Model B coefficients; averaging over different locale compositions could explain them. This verifies an interpretive incompatibility, not a calculation error.
- School size and locale coefficients are associations, and the zero-inflated model's latent component does not directly measure institutional capacity (pp. 6, 8–11). Staffing, demand, community priorities, and policy effects remain explanations or proposals rather than mechanisms established by this design (pp. 19–21).
- The broad abstract statement about lower rural/town availability in 'the likelihood of offering each course' (p. 1) needs the Results qualification 'with the exception of AP Calculus AB' (p. 14; p. 16, Table 4). The literature review also confirms a denominator error in the background: Boles's school-based characterization of Mann et al. should be read as student access, as shown in that report's original tables (Boles, p. 5, narrative; [Mann et al., p. 5, Tables 1–2](https://www.ecs.org/wp-content/uploads/Advanced-Placement-Access-and-Success-How-do-rural-schools-stack-up.pdf)).
- Exact reproduction is limited by unspecified linkage and missing-data decisions, log-offset constants, and prediction procedures (pp. 5–7, 11–12, 21). Local spatial fits are less trustworthy than the national tables because bandwidth details, local support, and uncertainty are not supplied, and the author acknowledges sparsity and multicollinearity (pp. 17–18, Figures 10–11; p. 21, note 4). The access guide and online supplements were not assessed; raw-data restrictions themselves are not evidence of poor practice.

#### What to Rely On

- Historical school-level authorization disparities: 48.02% of rural schools and 79.08% of suburban schools had at least one authorized AP STEM course; the printed counts reproduce these percentages (p. 7, Table 1). These are shares of schools in the study frame, not student access rates.
- Less breadth in rural and town authorized AP STEM curricula: the descriptive ordering persists across the course-count thresholds, independently of the zero-inflated model (p. 7, Table 1).
- Subject-specific conditional associations: rural and town coefficients are negative for Calculus BC and advanced physics, positive for Calculus AB, and close to zero for Biology (p. 16, Table 4). The town Calculus AB estimate is imprecise; the positive point estimate should not be treated as a firmly established advantage.
- A finer-grained contribution to an established question: the article extends the prior research it discusses through school-level and subject-specific comparisons (pp. 2–5; p. 14, Table 3; p. 16, Table 4). This is an evaluative judgment about its contribution, not an independently verified priority claim.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Actual or current student access, participation, learning, and advanced STEM provision across all pathways: none is established by the pooled AP authorization measure (p. 5, Measures; p. 20, Limitations). The student-weighted supplementary analysis mentioned on p. 8 is not bound into the supplied PDF and could not be checked.
- The claim that comparable suburban schools offer nearly three times as many courses as rural schools: the p. 12 narrative predictions based on Table 2 (p. 10) do not document comparable covariate/state distributions, and their ratio is incompatible with that interpretation of the printed model.
- A causal explanation in terms of school size or geography, or a measured deficit in institutional capacity: covariate adjustment and a latent mixture model do not identify these claims (pp. 6, 8–11; p. 10, Table 2).
- Precise local rankings, geographic reversals, or intervention targets inferred from the spatial maps: the local fits lack the reported diagnostics and uncertainty needed for those uses, and omit the national models' state fixed effects (p. 15; pp. 17–18, Figures 10–11; p. 21, note 4).
- Claims that particular delivery models or resource policies will close the gaps: the discussion proposes explanations and responses, but this study does not evaluate their effects or adjudicate substitution between AP and other programs (pp. 19–21).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods, contribution, and reproducibility: Table 1's locale counts total 21,139 schools; 3,826/7,967 rural schools and 4,101/5,186 suburban schools reproduce 48.02% and 79.08%, and subtraction yields 7,982 schools with no authorization (p. 7, Table 1; corresponding narrative, p. 8).
- CONFIRMED — Writing and contribution: the abstract's 'likelihood of offering each course' (p. 1) requires the Results exception 'with the exception of AP Calculus AB' (p. 14); the rural and town log-odds estimates are .253 and .164, while Biology estimates are −.024 and −.049 (p. 16, Table 4). The town Calculus AB estimate has SE .100 and no significance marker, so its direction is a point-estimate finding.
- CONFIRMED — Methods: Model B prints rural coefficients −.363 for the structural-zero logit and −.152 for the count component (p. 10, Table 2); my algebra gives a common-profile rural/suburban overall-mean ratio between exp(−.152) = .859 and exp(−.152 + .363) = 1.235, incompatible with 1.81/5.35 = .338 from the p. 12 narrative predictions. This confirms the review's conditional incompatibility, not that the predictions themselves were miscalculated.
- CONFIRMED — Literature: Boles writes '92% of city schools' and '88% offered at least one STEM AP course' (p. 5, narrative, no accompanying exhibit); the cited source labels the denominator 'Percent of all seniors' and reports those urban entries in its Tables 1–2 (Mann et al., p. 5). The sub-review's correction is accurate: these are student percentages. [Original report](https://www.ecs.org/wp-content/uploads/Advanced-Placement-Access-and-Success-How-do-rural-schools-stack-up.pdf).
- CONFIRMED — Methods and reproducibility: the national models include state fixed effects, the local models omit them (p. 15), and note 4 explicitly cites local multicollinearity and sparse data (p. 21); this supports treating Figures 10–11 (pp. 17–18) as exploratory, a methodological judgment rather than proof that every mapped contrast is wrong.
- CONFIRMED — Reproducibility: the article explicitly states a data-use restriction and links an access guide (p. 21, Open Practices); log-offset constants and the complete reconstruction/prediction protocol are not specified in the supplied paper (pp. 5–7, 11–12).
- COULD NOT CHECK — The actual averaging procedure behind the overall predictions (p. 12, based on p. 10, Table 2), the student-weighted supplementary figure mentioned on p. 8, and the linked access guide's contents or availability of study code; online supplements and appendices are unavailable unless bound into the supplied PDF. No raw-data replication was performed.

The sub-reviews agree on the main evidentiary hierarchy; none of the checked claims required reversal. Their favorable assessments of coverage and subject detail are compatible with their concerns about interpretation and reproducibility: national descriptive authorization patterns deserve more weight than capacity explanations, absolute adjusted predictions, or precise local diagnoses. Confidence below is each sub-review’s confidence in its assessment, not a probability that the paper’s claims are true.

| Methods | adequate | high (0.91) |
